text: The bay lies quiet under a waning gibbous moon, the water near its warmest for the year, though that warmth arrived a week late by the record and the whole summer has carried that lag forward. Joe-pye weed stands tall in the low ground along the bay shore, its dusky-rose heads just opening where the soil stays wet. Goldenrod has begun to show gold along the roadsides north toward the AuSable country, later than most Augusts allow. Katydids have taken up their nighttime rasp in the shrub edges. Trico spinners are due on the AuSable in the early morning hours, small and pale above the slow pools. A snowy egret works the shallows. Walleye have dropped to the deep basin. Walk a wet meadow margin at dusk and listen for the first katydid to go quiet.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, its surface the color of old pewter where cloud shadow crosses it. Lake Huron is at or near its annual high, and the warmth that has built since May now peaks in soil and water alike, though seven days behind where the record says it should be. Joe-Pye weed stands tall in the wet margins along the Thumb roads, its dusky-rose heads just opening, a week later than a normal year would show. Goldenrod is breaking into first bloom along those same roadsides. After dark, the first katydids should be audible in the shrubby edges. Whitetail bucks carry their velvet racks into the August browse. Walk any alder run feeding the AuSable before dawn and listen for the thin, rising rasp of katydids beginning their long argument with the night.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, barely a ripple crossing the shallows off Quanicassee, and the water has reached its annual high. Seven days behind the record, August is doing its work slowly. Joe-Pye weed stands head-high in the wet ditches along Rinde Road, its dusky-rose heads just opening where they should have opened the week before. Goldenrod is breaking yellow along the field edges, though a normal year would show it further along by now. At night the katydids have taken up their rasping, the surest sound of summer turning. White-tailed bucks carry full velvet racks in the oak edges north toward the AuSable. Walk any riverside wet meadow at first light and look for trico spinners hovering in slow columns above the current.

The bay lies nearly flat under a full moon that sets just as the trico spinners begin their morning fall above the slower AuSable backwaters. Seven days behind the record, goldenrod has only now opened its first heads along M-55, and joe-pye weed stands in the wet ditches with its dusky-rose crowns just reaching their best. Katydids have taken up their rasping in the oaks after dark, marking the turn more honestly than any calendar. Whitetail bucks carry velvet racks still weeks from hardening. Walleye have dropped to deep cool water in the bay, absent from the shallows. The trico hatch is the thing to watch: be on the river at first light, look for the spinner fall in slow water where riffles ease into pools.

The bay lies nearly flat this morning, its surface the color of old pewter under a new moon. Lake Huron is at or near its annual high, and the warm shallows along the Thumb hold that late-summer stillness that comes just before things begin to move the other way. Seven days behind, the season has pushed goldenrod and joe-pye weed later than their usual August opening, but both are underway now along any low wet margin from Caseville north toward the AuSable country. Katydids are rasping in the dark. Whitetail bucks are still carrying velvet. On the AuSable in the gray hour before sunrise, trico spinners are worth watching above the riffles, where the tiny flies gather and fall in their brief window before the light comes full.
